https://www.politico.eu/article/job-volo.text: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has a problem: Nobody wants the hardest job in Washington. The Ukrainian president is struggling to find someone of sufficient influence to represent Kyiv to the Trump administration, with prospective candidates proving reluctant to take on the grueling assignment at a critical moment in the war, according to two former senior Ukrainian officials and four lawmakers. The need to replace the previous envoy, Olga Stefanishyna, helped trigger Zelenskyy’s still-incomplete government reshuffle. Stefanishyna was formally dismissed on Aug. 3 over impending embezzlement charges. Advertisement Advertisement Zelenskyy moved his reshuffle plans forward so he could offer the ambassadorship to Yulia Svyrydenko, the outgoing prime minister, according to a former senior Ukrainian official and a Republican foreign expert familiar with the background to the shake-up. But she declined , disrupting his plans. “It is no secret that I counted on and offered Yulia Svyrydenko the post of ambassador to the United States,” Zelenskyy said at a press conference in late July. He added that he was looking for a candidate with the highest possible qualifications: “a person at the level of a deputy prime minister, minister, or prime minister.” Since then, however, other prospective candidates have proved equally reluctant, spurning what would in any case be the difficult job of handling Donald Trump’s unpredictable White House. Ukrainians with sufficient heft and skill for the ambassadorship are looking at it askance, “worrying that they would not enjoy the conditions they would need to do the job properly,” said Ivanna Klympush-Tsintsadze, a prominent Ukrainian opposition lawmaker and former deputy prime minister who is a regular critic of Zelenskyy. “Certainly that would be the case without having the ear of the president or his trust,” she added. That narrows Zelenskyy’s options sharply. The person would likely have to come from his tight inner circle of trusted aides, Klympush-Tsintsadze said, but there is no one there who seriously fits the bill. “Framing it as if nobody wants the job would be a kind of oversimplification,” said a former Ukrainian diplomat who was granted anonymity in order to speak freely. “Of course, there are people who want the job, but there’s no one who really measures up to it. Zelenskyy is having a hard time filling the position.” Advertisement Advertisement Wrong direction The trouble filling the Washington post is part of a broader problem for Zelenskyy, whose office did not respond to a request for comment. The president’s approval ratings have deteriorated since he embarked a month ago on a government shake-up that remains incomplete and has proved turbulent. According to a Socis Center for Social Research survey, more than 55 percent of Ukrainians believe their nation is moving in the wrong direction. Zelenskyy’s dismissal in July of popular defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov sparked street protests and a political backlash, while several key posts remain unresolved. The reshuffle has also raised questions about how Zelenskyy chooses his senior team — and how far beyond his tight circle of trusted aides he is prepared to look. “No one has explained to Ukrainians why exactly the government had to be changed,” Mykola Knyazhitskiy, an opposition lawmaker from Lviv and founder of Ukraine’s Espreso TV channel, said. Yulia Svyrydenko looks on during a press conference in Kyiv on March 3, 2026. | Tetiana Dzhafarova/AFP via Getty Images “There had been no clearly articulated public complaints about Svyrydenko. In her farewell address to parliament, Svyrydenko received applause. MPs gave her a standing ovation. So why was she dismissed if her performance was considered so successful and was so highly regarded?” Difficult timing The ambassadorial vacancy comes at an especially fraught moment for Kyiv. Washington remains central to Ukraine’s ability to sustain the war, and whoever takes the job will have to navigate a Trump administration that has repeatedly shifted course on military support and on how — and when — the war should end. In an interview with POLITICO’s Dasha Burns earlier this year, Stefanishyna acknowledged she had experienced “diplomatic whiplash” in the role. Advertisement Advertisement Kyiv is trying to persuade Trump to give Ukraine a license to manufacture Patriot air defense systems , something he promised in June, only to reverse himself in July. The issue is becoming more urgent as Ukraine heads toward another winter of Russian attacks on its energy and civilian infrastructure and is already struggling to intercept intensified ballistic missile strikes. Zelenskyy has said this year’s deliveries of air defense missiles from Ukraine’s allies have fallen by two-thirds compared with 2025. At the same time, there are signs the White House may soon seek to revive stalled peace negotiations. That would put a premium on having an ambassador in Washington with the political weight to get through the door, the authority to speak for Zelenskyy and the skill to navigate an administration where policy can change quickly. And also to lobby Congress. Leaving the post vacant, therefore, carries risks well beyond diplomatic protocol. Ukraine could find itself without a heavyweight operator in Washington just as decisions are being made over weapons, air defense, logistics and intelligence sharing, as well as the terms of any renewed peace push. “It is quite likely that Zelenskyy won’t appoint anyone this side of the midterm elections in the United States,” said Yaroslav Yurchyshyn, an opposition lawmaker. “It will be hard to judge who would fit the political landscape best until those elections have been held.”

https://www.dw.com/en/myanmar-military-a.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JFBa According to war observers, Myanmar's military is increasingly targeting public buildings Image: Ko Nway Oo/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement At least 14 people were killed when a military airstrike hit a Buddhist monastery in Myanmar's central Sagaing region, an opposition group and local witnesses said Saturday. Friday's attack, by the ruling military regime that seized power in a 2021 coup, is the latest deadly assault on pro-democracy forces in the Southeast Asian country's ongoing civil war. What do we know about the airstrike on the monastery in Myanmar? The strike happened in Swel Le Oh village, Myaung township, in central Myanmar, said Nway Oo, a spokesman for an anti-government resistance group. The village is about 75 kilometers (45 miles) west of Mandalay, the country's second largest city. Nway Oo, from the Civil Defense and Security Organization of Myaung Township, or CDSOM, said the dead included three women and that 20 others were wounded. The Associated Press spoke to a villager who confirmed the death toll and said that a military jet dropped two bombs 15 minutes apart. The villager said the second strike damaged a nearby house. Victims were civilians attending a retreat More than 100 people were taking part in a weeklong meditation retreat to mark Buddhist Lent, the villager added. AFP news agency cited Nway Oo Myaung, a pro-democracy rebel, as saying: "It wasn't a mistaken target; they intentionally attacked a monastery." The military government has yet to confirm the strike. Myanmar's military has often used airstrikes to counter opposition forces, especially in Sagaing region, a stronghold of armed resistance. Myanmar's most recent coup ended a transition to democracy than began in 2011 Image: Ko Nway Oo/AP Photo/picture alliance UN flags sharp rise in airstrikes A United Nations investigation team said last week it had observed a notable increase in aerial attacks over much of the past year. The UN's Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM) accused the military-backed government of "indiscriminate and intentional aerial attacks against civilians." Last month, conflict monitoring group ACLED accused the regime of adopting "a terror strategy" that it said focuses on "civilian infrastructure and social gatherings, such as weddings and religious festivals, to maximize psychological impact." Myanmar government defends strikes On Sunday, Myanmar’s foreign ministry rejected the IIMM report, insisting that its operations were in response to insurgents and terrorist groups. The ministry said it uses maximum restraint to avoid civilian harm. Myanmar's army took power from the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in February 2021. Suu Kyi, a Nobel Peace Prize laureate, was detained and sentenced to lengthy prison terms on multiple charges widely viewed as politically motivated. She was moved to house arrest in May. Aung San Suu Kyi's son on the latest images of his mother To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video After a brutal crackdown on peaceful demonstrations, many opponents of military rule armed themselves and plunged large parts of the country into conflict. More than 100,000 people are estimated to have been killed on all sides over the past five years, according to ACLED. Myanmar held elections this year, which were widely condemned as a sham . The polls culminated in the chief of the former junta, General Min Aung Hlaing, being appointed president, as the military regime sought to present itself as a civilian government. Photograph: US Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Ohio View image in fullscreen Seized jewelry in connection with the romance scam. Photograph: US Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Ohio US crime Three plead guilty in $9m romance fraud scam targeting elderly Americans Twin brothers, 22, from Ghana and a 53-year-old American woman targeted older adults in 25 US states, officials say Maya Yang Wed 28 Oct 2026 12.57 EDT Last modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 13.12 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Three people have pleaded guilty in a $9m romance fraud scam that targeted elderly Americans. On Monday, the US attorney’s office in the northern district of Ohio announced that twin brothers from Ghana and an American woman pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud. Identified as Jamal Abubakari, Kamal Abubakari, both 22, and Amanda Joy Opoku-Boachie, 53, of Kula, Hawaii, the trio targeted more than 130 victims in 25 states, as well as in Germany and Austria. The Abubakaris and Opoku-Boachie targeted older Americans on dating websites and social media platforms from July 2024 to April 2026, conspiring with others to “fake personas to establish close, personal relationships with the victims which were often romantic in nature”, according to the justice department. The trio at times used “artificial intelligence-driven video platforms to engage victims under fictitious female personas”, the justice department said. The victims, after being misled by false stories, would then wire money to bank accounts controlled by the conspiracy members, with portions of the funds also being distributed to co-conspirators in Ghana and elsewhere. As part of their scheme, the trio said they allegedly needed the money for medical emergencies, investment opportunities or travel fees to visit the victims, according to court documents reviewed by outlets. “Victims report that they are left with absolutely nothing to sustain their lives going forward after a lifetime of work and saving. In addition, individual victims are ashamed and deprived of the trust they once had in their fellow human beings,” prosecutors said in the documents. In total, the victims lost more than $9m, the justice department said. As part of their plea agreement, the Abubakaris and Opoku-Boachie agreed to forfeit jewellry which investigators seized at the time of their arrests, including luxury timepieces, as well as high-end watches, rings, chains, medallions and earrings. They face a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison, with sentencing for the brothers scheduled for 9 February 2027 and 10 February 2027 for Opoku-Boachie. Other co-conspirators are awaiting extradition from Ghana where seized assets estimated to be worth more than $3m include a Lamborghini, a Tesla Cybertruck, a Mercedes-Benz and a BMW, the justice department said. Composite: Getty Images ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) Democratic lawmakers demand ICE data on detainee miscarriages Demand comes after Guardian investigation found ICE failed to record data on miscarriages suffered by immigrants in its custody between October 2025 and June 2026 Maanvi Singh Fri 30 Oct 2026 19.01 EDT Last modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 19.55 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google US lawmakers are urgently demanding that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) disclose how many pregnant immigrants have experienced miscarriages, stillbirths and pregnancy-related hospitalizations while in the its custody, after the agency admitted it lost count last year. US representatives sent the request following a recent Guardian investigation revealing that the Trump administration is detaining a record number of pregnant women and teens, and at the same has lost track of how many suffered miscarriages. Revealed: ICE lost count of miscarriages, while detaining a record number of pregnant women Read more In a letter sent this month to ICE’s acting director, David Venturella, Democratic representatives Brittany Pettersen, Joyce Beatty and Robin Kelly also asked the immigration enforcement agency to explain what – if any – steps have been taken to recover any missing data about these cases. Government documents obtained by the Guardian found that ICE had placed more pregnant immigrants in detention last fall and winter than at any time over the previous year. The agency recorded 18 miscarriages during the first nine months of the Trump administration, the documents found, but the agency has no data on miscarriages after 3 October 2025. Detained pregnant women said that they were struggling to access routine and emergency medical care. Medical experts told the Guardian that lapses in care both during pregnancy and during and after miscarriage could escalate treatable conditions into life-threatening emergencies. In their letter, the representatives also cite a 2021 directive instructing ICE to wholly avoid detaining pregnant, postpartum and nursing immigrants “unless release is prohibited by law or exceptional circumstances exist” – and ask the agency to clarify on what grounds it is detaining pregnant immigrants. The directive also requires ICE to closely monitor and document the health of all pregnant people in its custody, and continuously evaluate whether it is medically advisable to keep them detained. “ICE’s inability to follow agency directives, provide adequate medical care and maintain accurate records of pregnancy-related medical outcomes is unacceptable,” the lawmakers wrote in their letter, which was cosigned by 64 other representatives. In an interview, Pettersen said it was “deeply concerning” that ICE had failed to account for a full year of pregnancy outcomes. “I’m just devastated for the people who have gone through this, who’ve lost pregnancies unnecessarily, who have been left without the medical care that they need after miscarrying,” she said. “It’s hard to imagine how we are ever going to right these wrongs.” In internal agency documents, ICE said it had no data on miscarriages because the agency changed medical billing providers in October. The agency’s medical claims processing has been delayed for months. Immigration attorneys and former government officials told said it was odd, but plausible, that ICE was keeping track of miscarriages solely via its medical billing provider. In response to follow-up questions about its tracking practices after 3 October 2025, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, first said that the agency was tracking miscarriages in monthly reports. But later, the spokesperson confirmed what was in the ICE internal documents – the agency does not have data on miscarriages between October 2025 through June 2026. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Around 2-3 times a day Sign up to Breaking News US Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion The DHS did not confirm to the Guardian whether it had received the letter from Congress members. “Claims that any pregnant detainees are receiving subprime care are FALSE,” an agency spokesperson said. In their letter, lawmakers asked ICE’s acting director to detail when “ICE leadership first became aware of concerns regarding miscarriage reporting and deficiencies in agency tracking systems”. They gave the agency until 6 November to respond. Prior to the Guardian’s reporting, the agency had never acknowledged that it had lost count of miscarriages – not even when US senators asked the agency for the data. The Guardian filed a Freedom of Information Act request and then filed suit in collaboration with the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press to obtain data on the number of pregnant people in ICE detention, and the health outcomes for this population. https://www.portfolio.hu/global/20261109.text: Az orosz állami média Alan Lusnyikovra, a Kalasnyikov-konszern vezérigazgatójára hivatkozva számolt be arról, hogy a Krona légvédelmi rakétarendszer sikeresen teljesítette az idén tavasztól őszig tartó előzetes próbákat. A fegyverrendszert elsődlegesen arra tervezték, hogy megvédje a kiemelt fontosságú létesítményeket a nagy hatótávolságú ukrán csapásmérő drónoktól. A tájékoztatás szerint a rendszer most kapja meg az "O" jelölést, ami az orosz hadiipari terminológiában a kísérleti nullszéria, vagyis az első prototípusok legyártásának szakaszát jelenti. Ez egyúttal azt is mutatja, hogy az eszköz jelenleg még nem áll készen a sorozatgyártásra. A vállalat közlése szerint a Kronát most készítik fel az állami tesztekre, amelyek akár még az idei év vége előtt megkezdődhetnek. Az előzetes tesztek elindulását még idén április közepén jelentették be az oroszok. Akkor azt állították, hogy a próbák a valós harci viszonyokat modellezik, ám azt továbbra sem tudni, hogy az orosz csapatok élesben, ukrán drónok ellen is kipróbálták-e az eszközt, vagy csupán lőtéri gyakorlatokról volt szó. A Krona valójában nem egy teljesen új fejlesztés, hanem a korábbi Szoszna légvédelmi rakétarendszer átnevezett változata. Ez utóbbit eredetileg a szovjet eredetű Sztrela–10-esek váltótípusának szánták, ám végül soha nem rendszeresítették az orosz hadseregben. Moszkva mindenesetre komoly exportlehetőséget lát a fegyverben. Ezt bizonyítja, hogy Oroszország már tavaly bemutatta az eszköz Krona–E jelű exportváltozatát a Független Államok Közössége (FÁK) védelmi miniszteri tanácsának légvédelmi koordinációs bizottsága előtt.
